entities.name: Peregrine Laziosi
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Peregrine Laziosi (c. 1260 – May 1, 1345) was an Italian mendicant friar of the Servite Order, canonized as a saint in 1726. His life, marked by a profound conversion, rigorous asceticism, and a renowned miraculous healing, established him as a significant figure in late medieval Italian Catholicism, particularly venerated for his intercession on behalf of the gravely ill. His narrative reflects the broader spiritual currents of 13th and 14th-century Italy, where mendicant orders played a crucial role in popular piety and social welfare, offering spiritual guidance and tangible service to communities amidst political and social upheaval.

Born in Forlì, Romagna, Peregrine's early life was entangled with the region's intense Guelph-Ghibelline conflicts. Initially an ardent anti-papal Guelph, he famously struck Saint Philip Benizi, then prior general of the Servites, during a civic disturbance in Forlì. Benizi's patient and forgiving response profoundly impacted Peregrine, leading to his conversion and subsequent entry into the Servite Order in Siena around 1283. He dedicated over 60 years to prayer, penance, and ministry, becoming known for his austere lifestyle, including a purported vow never to sit for 30 years. In his later life, a severe leg ulcer, widely believed to be cancerous, threatened amputation; however, Peregrine experienced a miraculous healing the night before the scheduled surgery, attributing it to a vision of Christ, an event that cemented his reputation for sanctity.
